_doc: THE CIRCLE INVARIANT, as a CHECKER rather than as two more vectors.
THE LAW. For any Shift-constrained draw, at ANY zoom and ANY pan, the
committed element is SQUARE BIT-EXACTLY:
ellipse.rx == ellipse.ry        (a circle)
rect.width == rect.height       (a square)
Not 'within an epsilon'. `==` on the raw doubles. A circle is a circle
only if the two radii are the SAME double: the model types the shape by
comparing them, the SVG writer rounds them to 4 decimal places and so
cannot show a gap, and an artist who drew a circle and reopened an
ellipse has been lied to. There is no tolerance band in which that is
acceptable, so the checker admits none.
WHY A CHECKER AND NOT MORE VECTORS. DYADICSIDE (2026-07-30) fixed the
cause -- the constrained side is CARRIED in tool state (`doc_w`/`doc_h`)
instead of RECOVERED by re-subtracting the anchor -- but pinned it with
two hand-picked gesture fixtures. That is far weaker than it looks. The
round trip `(anchor + side) - anchor` only loses an ulp when the sum
CROSSES A BINADE, so most candidate vectors come back exact BY LUCK: of
eleven plausible hand-authored vectors tried while writing this file,
ONE was red under the old spelling. The original defect needed a
SEARCHED-FOR vector to expose it, which is precisely the signature of a
property that wants fuzzing, not enumeration.
So this file is read by three lanes, in the ruled order -- the checker is
the law, the corpus is its witnesses, the generative lane is its growing
confidence:
1. THE CHECKER. A predicate over (zoom, pan, press, release) that
replays the gesture through the production CanvasTool seam and
rules the committed element legal or illegal. It lives in code
(Rust `check_shift_constrain`, Swift `checkShiftConstrain`) because
it is a law, not data.
2. `witnesses` below -- named vectors the checker runs every CI run,
deterministically. Nine of the eleven are SEARCHED, not guessed.
3. `generative` below -- parameters for a seeded input stream that
re-runs the same checker on FRESH vectors each CI run.
THE MUTANT, and why `discriminating` is a field and not a comment. A
checker that cannot fail the bug it was written for is worth zero. Both
runners therefore carry `dyadicside_mutant` -- eight lines of arithmetic
reproducing the PRE-DYADICSIDE spelling (`abs(doc_end - doc_start)`,
the radius recovered from the coordinate) -- and assert, on every
witness, that the mutant's verdict matches the `discriminating` flag
recorded here. The generative lane makes the same measurement on its
fresh sample and refuses a run in which fewer than
`min_discriminating` of the generated vectors could have caught the
bug. The teeth are therefore checked continuously, not once by hand.
The mutant is NOT a second copy of the implementation. It is the BUG,
written down. If the tools' constraint arithmetic ever changes shape,
the mutant must be re-derived or deleted outright -- a stale mutant
measures nothing while looking like it measures something.
TWO NON-DISCRIMINATING WITNESSES ARE KEPT ON PURPOSE
(`identity_view_smoke`, `zoom_out_tenth`). They are the shape of the
hand smoke test that passed while the feature was broken everywhere
else: at zoom 1 every doc coordinate is dyadic, and at zoom 0.1 the
quotients keep enough trailing zeros that the sum never rounds. They
cover the extreme-zoom ends of the range AND stand as the recorded
reason the corpus needed a generator.
SETUP AND READING. Every case runs against `svg/empty_layer.svg` -- one
empty layer -- so the committed element is the only child, at path
[0, 0]. Screen coordinates are viewport pixels; the tools convert with
`doc = (screen - view_offset) / zoom` (YamlTool's pointer_event_payload,
identical in both ports). The gesture is always press / move(shift) /
release(shift) at the same release point.
THE 1-PIXEL COMMIT GUARD. Both tools suppress a draw whose constrained
screen extent is <= 1 px on either axis. Every witness clears it, and
the generator's `drag_min` is set so that every generated vector clears
it too -- so both runners assert that an element WAS committed. A
property that silently checks nothing is the failure mode this whole
file exists to avoid.
_tools_doc: The two Shift-constrained draw tools and the field pair each must make
equal. `fields` names the pair in the SAME explicit field table the
Swift `gestureExactField`), so a tool naming a field that table does
not carry fails loudly instead of asserting nothing.
_witnesses_doc: [x, y] viewport pixels, and `discriminating` -- whether the
PRE-DYADICSIDE spelling gets this vector WRONG. `discriminating` is
asserted against the mutant every run; it is a measurement, not a note.

witnesses.name: dyadicside_ellipse_zoom_1_5
witnesses.why: The original DYADICSIDE vector, searched for. At zoom 1.5 the doc-space anchor 100/3 is not dyadic, 100/3 + 60 crosses the 64 binade, and the old spelling recovered ry = 30.000000000000004 against rx = 30.0.

witnesses.name: identity_view_smoke
witnesses.why: The SAME drag at 100% zoom with no pan -- the hand smoke test that passed while every other viewport was broken. Every doc coordinate is an exact integer, so the round trip is exact BY LUCK. Kept as the recorded reason a generator was needed.

witnesses.name: horizontal_drag_leftward_zoom_1_5
witnesses.why: A PURE HORIZONTAL Shift drag (release y == press y), dragged LEFTWARD so the x branch takes the negative sign. The vertical direction has no sign to follow and takes the positive branch, so the anchor round trip runs on an axis the cursor never moved along. Searched.

witnesses.name: vertical_drag_upward_zoom_7_3
witnesses.why: The mirror case: a PURE VERTICAL drag of only 5 px at a deep zoom, committing a shape of radius ~0.34 doc units. Small shapes are where an absolute-epsilon comparison would have hidden the gap. Searched.

witnesses.name: up_left_quadrant_zoom_7_3
witnesses.why: Both signs negative -- the shape grows up and to the left of the anchor, so both axes take the `0 - side` branch. Searched.

witnesses.name: up_right_quadrant_zoom_5_5
witnesses.why: Mixed signs (right and up), and the constrained side comes from the SHORTER screen axis being overridden by the longer one. Searched.

witnesses.name: panned_integer_offsets_zoom_3
witnesses.why: A PANNED view: the pan enters the anchor before the divide, so it changes which binade the sum lands in. Integer offsets, so the pan itself is exact and only the zoom is to blame. Searched.

witnesses.name: panned_fractional_offsets_zoom_0_75
witnesses.why: A panned view at a zoom BELOW 1 with fractional (eighth-pixel) offsets -- the state a trackpad pan actually leaves the view in. Searched.

witnesses.name: two_pixel_drag_zoom_1_1
witnesses.why: The SMALLEST drag that survives the 1-pixel commit guard: 2 px on both axes. The committed radius is ~0.909 doc units and the gap is ~3.6e-15 -- five orders of magnitude below the 4-dp golden's resolution. Searched.

witnesses.name: full_viewport_drag_zoom_1_5
witnesses.why: The largest drag the 800x600 viewport allows, corner to corner. Confirms the invariant is not a small-numbers accident. Searched.

witnesses.name: zoom_out_tenth
witnesses.why: The far zoomed-OUT end of the range: a 424 px drag becomes a 4240 doc-unit shape. Dividing an integer by 0.1 leaves enough trailing zeros in the mantissa that the sum never rounds, so this vector is exact even under the old spelling -- a second recorded example of luck, and the low-zoom coverage the searched vectors do not reach.

_generative_doc: THE GENERATIVE LANE. Parameters for the seeded input stream both ports
spell identically, so a seed that goes red in one replays in the other.
The seed is FRESH EVERY RUN (nanosecond clock), not fixed: the point is
to see vectors nobody chose. It is printed at the head of every run and
again on failure, and `JAS_PROPERTY_SEED=<u64>` in the environment
replaces it, so a red is exactly reproducible.
One case draws NINE values from the stream, in this order -- both ports
must consume them in the same order or the two streams diverge:
1 zoom       lerp(zoom_min, zoom_max)
2 offset x   lerp(offset_min, offset_max)
3 offset y   lerp(offset_min, offset_max)
4 press x    lerp(press_min, press_max)
5 press y    lerp(press_min, press_max)
6 drag dx    signed magnitude in [drag_min, drag_max]
7 drag dy    signed magnitude in [drag_min, drag_max]
8 axis lock  < axis_zero_p -> dy = 0; < 2*axis_zero_p -> dx = 0
9 quantize   < quantize_p  -> round all four screen coords to integers
NO REJECTION SAMPLING. The drag is built as an offset FROM the press
rather than as an independent second point, so `drag_min` guarantees
every generated vector clears the 1-pixel commit guard (rounding can
shave at most 1 px, and drag_min is 3). Every draw is therefore a real
case, and both runners assert that the number of elements committed
equals the number of cases -- the generator cannot quietly degrade into
asserting nothing.
The axis lock exists because a pure horizontal or vertical Shift drag
takes a different branch: the zero axis has no sign to follow, so it
takes the positive one, and the anchor round trip runs on an axis the
cursor never moved along. A continuous generator produces an exact zero
with probability zero, so it has to be asked for.
The quantize lock exists because real pointer events are usually
integral, and integral screen coordinates are a MEASURABLY different
population: at zoom 0.1, 1/3 and 1.0 they are exact under the old
spelling where continuous ones are not.
min_discriminating is the floor on how many of the `cases` generated
vectors the mutant says the PRE-DYADICSIDE spelling would get wrong. It
is a live measurement of the lane's teeth. Measured over 40 random
seeds at these parameters: 81 to 118 of 384, mean 101. The floor of 20
sits about nine standard deviations below that mean -- far enough that
tripping it means the generator has been narrowed or broken, not that a
run was unlucky.
_stream_pin_doc: A cross-language pin on the STREAM ITSELF, so 'replay this seed in the
other port' is a guarantee rather than a hope. Both runners build the
stream at `seed`, draw the first three cases, and compare them to these
values EXACTLY. If it goes red, the two ports are no longer fuzzing the
same space and every seed exchanged between them is meaningless.
THE VALUES ARE IEEE-754 BIT PATTERNS AS HEX STRINGS, NOT DECIMAL
LITERALS, AND THAT IS NOT FUSSINESS. Measured while writing this file,
on serde_json 1.0.149 with default features -- the configuration
jas_dioxus builds today:
serde_json mis-parses 21397 of 199903 SHORTEST-ROUND-TRIP f64
literals by exactly 1 ulp (10.7%).
It is not a long-literal problem. `1.1929870363539823` -- seventeen
significant digits, the shortest form that round-trips, and the second
case's zoom below -- reads back as `...825` in Rust. Rust's own
`str::parse::<f64>()` reads it correctly, Swift's JSONSerialization
reads it correctly, and `Double(String)` reads it correctly; it is
serde_json's default float path, which is fast rather than
correctly-rounded. (`serde_json`'s `float_roundtrip` feature fixes it:
0 of 199903 with the feature on. That is a build decision, not this
fixture's to make.)
So a full-precision DECIMAL pin in a shared fixture is not a shared
value at all: one port in ten reads a different double than the other,
silently, and a bit-exactness gate built on it would report phantom
reds and phantom greens with equal confidence. A bit-exact property
gets pinned by bits. `_decimal` beside each case is for human eyes and
is never compared.
Hex STRINGS rather than integers because a negative double's bit
pattern exceeds 2^63, which JSONSerialization would hand back as a
Double and quietly ruin. Both ports parse these with a plain
radix-16 integer parse.
